definition: Rhetorical structure theory (RST) is a theory of text organization that describes relations that hold between parts of text.
details: It was originally developed by William Mann, Sandra Thompson, Christian M. I. M. Matthiessen and others at the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute (ISI) and defined in a 1988 paper. The theory was developed as part of studies of computer-based text generation. Natural language processing researchers later began using RST in automatic summarization and other applications. It explains coherence by postulating a hierarchical, connected structure of texts, which are labeled using a small, predefined inventory of relation types - for example, one part of a text may provide an elaboration on another part, provide background or specify a cause for another. In the 2000s, following the release of the first large-scale dataset implementing the theory, the RST Discourse Treebank (RST-DT), Daniel Marcu demonstrated the feasibility of practical applications of RST to discourse parsing and summarization at ISI. Originally limited to written text, subsequent work in the 2010s expanded RST to spoken language analysis, and the framework has been applied to a variety of languages including Persian, German, Mandarin Chinese, Russian and Spanish. Following the introduction of Transformers, LLMs have been applied to automatic RST parsing, with results approaching human performance on parsing text in English.

explainer.lead: Rhetorical structure theory (RST) is a theory of text organization that describes relations holding between parts of text. It matters because it explains textual coherence through a hierarchical, connected structure, which makes it usable for computational text processing.

tiers.eli5: Think of a paragraph as a building: some parts carry the main point and other parts support them, and RST is the blueprint showing how the pieces hold each other up.
tiers.practitioner: NLP engineers apply RST in automatic summarization and other tasks, using its relation structure to decide which spans are central. A pitfall is assuming one clean hierarchy when real texts may resist a single analysis.
tiers.paperLevel: Text is modeled as a hierarchical, connected structure in which spans of text stand in named relations to one another; the theory was defined in a 1988 paper and developed at USC's Information Sciences Institute.

explainer.example: In a short argumentative passage, one span states a claim and another gives evidence for it; RST records the evidence span as supporting the claim span within a larger hierarchy.
